title: Powerful habit changes for more inclusive teaching.
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington distills the habit changes that resonate most with teachers in his Big Classroom training, all aimed at systematically including every student and deepening their thinking. He argues that the ubiquitous 'can anyone tell me?' reinforces a vocal minority, and replaces it with cold calling framed as a warm invitation, followed by a second question to the same student. He adds A/B partner structures so quieter students share first, structured questions that demand several reasons with explanations, whole answers, and 'things to think with' such as diagrams and worked examples. Other routines include a second verification loop with show-me boards, praising 8 out of 10 before full marks to build a culture of error, paired rehearsal of explanations, and short model-and-check feedback loops. He closes by redefining whole-class discussion as a cycle of pairs, cold calls, volunteers, and back to pairs so that literally everyone is involved.
points: Asking for volunteers turns learning into a contest for attention; cold calling framed as an invitation makes everyone expect to think.
A follow-up question to the same student reveals the real thinking, since first responses are nearly always shallow.
Rechecking with a second show-me board loop confirms whether a quick reteach actually landed.
Asking who scored 7 or 8 out of 10 before praising full marks normalizes error and surfaces misconceptions.
True class discussion cycles through think-pair-share, cold calls, volunteers, and a return to pairs so all students participate.
quotes: Teachers are inviting students to volunteer and, effectively, reinforcing the dominance of a minority individuals at the expense of everyone else. Learning should not be a contest for attention; it’s the teacher’s job to orchestrate the room so that absolutely everyone feels included, with their attention focused on the learning in hand.
This always deepens their first response, tells you more about what they know and models to others that we’re going for depth, not accepting shallowness.
This means the second person largely hears ideas – or answers – from their partner before they’ve formed their own response. This isn’t ok.
You can’t think with knowledge you don’t have. This creates a sense of feeling stupid, stress, a dread of being asked etc.
Does this now mean everyone has heard, registered, absorbed and updated their schema? No! Not by a long way. As a minimum, do a quick verification check.
In contrast if you say ‘who got them all correct’ and a large number got 10/10 – the others feel stupid and tend to hide their errors.
Build it up step by step, with a high success rate at each step, before doing more extended more independent work.
The point is that inclusive discussion must involve everyone. It’s not enough to hope they’re listening.
